title: Absolute and conditional convergence
section: Alternating Series ▷ Absolute versus conditional convergence
terms: absolute convergence; conditional convergence; absolute convergence implies convergence; signed series.

exposition.text:
P P
A series a is absolutely convergent if |a | converges. Absolute convergence implies conver-
n n
gence. A convergent series is conditionally convergent when its absolute-value series diverges;
the alternating harmonic series is the standard example. A divergent series is neither absolutely
nor conditionally convergent.
Absolute convergence makes arbitrary bounded changes of signs harmless and permits rear-
rangement without changing the sum. Conditional convergence is more delicate: arbitrary rear-
rangement is not generally legitimate. If magnitudes have a convergent positive majorant, no
alternating pattern is needed. Conversely, failure of absolute convergence does not determine
whether the original signed series converges; analyze its cancellations separately.

solution.text:
The alternating test gives convergence for p > 0. The absolute series is a p-series, which
converges only for p > 1. Thus conditional convergence occurs exactly for 0 < p ≤ 1; at
p ≤ 0 the terms fail to tend to zero.

solution.text:
For every fixed p, the magnitudes eventually decrease to zero, so the alternating series
converges. Its absolute series converges exactly for p > 1 by the logarithmic integral test.
